Part 1 · The round

What does an outside operator do, and where does the round take them?

Part 1 · the plan

From a job description to a walked route

  1. The outside operator's jobread, check, operate, report: the console's eyes and hands
  2. Console says, field confirmswhy a transmitter alone is not the whole truth
  3. The 12-station round on the plot planwhere each station is, its level, what is read there
  4. Two working levelsgrade and the platform at EL 3.0, and how you move between them

The job

Four verbs: read, check, operate, report

Read

Local gauges and transmitter displays, by eye.

Check

What no instrument shows: sound, plume, heat, a trap cycling.

Operate

Hand valves and local pump buttons. Each move is a process change.

Report

Tag, value, normal value, what was done, to the console.

Every verb happens at a place. Before the places, the reason the console needs someone there.

Why a field round

Console says, field confirms

  • The DCS shows only what is transmitted.
  • Hand valves, traps, drains and vents have no transmitter.
  • A transmitter can be wrong; a second reading in the field settles it.

Section summary

What part 1 settled

  • The outside operator reads, checks, operates and reports.
  • The field sees what the DCS cannot: hand valves, traps, vents, drains, sound and heat.
  • Twelve stations follow water → steam → condensate; four of them are on the platform at EL 3.0.
  • Recognise each station by its shape; tags confirm.

Part 2 · Gauges and hand valves

What does a local gauge tell you, and what does a hand valve change?

Part 2 · the plan

Reading, then touching

  1. Local gauge against transmitterwhich variable has which, and who else uses it
  2. Reading a dialspan, division, interpolation, and a drill on random values
  3. The normal line-upblock valves open, bypasses, vents and drains closed

Two kinds of reading

A gauge is read where it stands

Local gauge (PG, TG)

Needle on a dial: only someone standing there sees it.

Transmitter (PT, TT, FT)

Sends the value to the DCS: trends, alarms, control, trips.

Interactive · measurement points

Which variable has a gauge, a transmitter, or both

Condensate temperature and return pressure exist only in the field; the outlet temperature has three independent readings.

Reading a dial

Span, division, interpolate

$$x = x_{lo} + \frac{\theta}{270^\circ}\,(x_{hi}-x_{lo})$$

The dial sweeps 270°, with ten divisions of $\tfrac{1}{10}(x_{hi}-x_{lo})$ each.

$x$
value read
kPa g or °C
$x_{lo},x_{hi}$
ends of the scale (dial range, assumed)
kPa g or °C
$\theta$
needle angle from the zero mark
°

Interactive · drill

Read the needle, then check

One division
Result
—

Values are random within each dial's middle range, not plant values. Interpolating to a quarter division (assumed tolerance) is good field reading.

Hand valves

Blocks open, bypasses, vents and drains closed

  • Block valves isolate a control valve for maintenance: NO.
  • A bypass, vent or drain lets fluid round or out: NC.
  • Both pumps keep suction and discharge open: the spare stays ready.

Fifteen hand valves follow these three rules. Next: what each one does when it is out of position.

Interactive · model runs

Move one valve, watch ten minutes

Each run is a copy of the model at design, the valve moved at 0 s, nobody acting after: the plant answers within seconds.

From the runs

Five principles behind fifteen valves

Valve movedWhat the model didPrinciple
Running pump's suction closedNever touch a running pump's suction
Running pump's discharge closedA dead-headed pump heats up
Block on a control valve closedClosed block, no flow
Control-valve bypass openedThe loop loses its range
Vent or drain openedSteam lost, silently

Section summary

What part 2 settled

  • Gauges are read only in the field; transmitters feed trends, alarms, control and trips.
  • Read a dial by its span and divisions, to a quarter division.
  • Normal line-up: blocks and pump valves open; bypasses, vents, drains closed.
  • A hand valve is a process change: trips in seconds, or a loss nobody alarms.

Part 3 · Naming and recording

How do you name what you see, record it, and catch a problem before an alarm does?

Part 3 · the plan

Name it, write it down, compare it

  1. Reading a tagletters say what is measured and what the device does
  2. Identificationnaming items without the tag plate, target 90 %
  3. The rounds sheet28 rows: numbers with a tolerance, states from a list
  4. Finding problems earlylosses the DCS never alarms, and how to report them

Interactive · identification

A tag is a sentence in letters

First letter: what is measured; the rest: what the device does; the number: its loop.

In the tab

Identify mode hides the plates

  • Type the tag in each box; Check, then Grade.
  • Target 90 %: 18 of 20.
  • Only letters and digits count; case is ignored.

Naming comes first; writing down what each item shows is the rounds sheet.

Interactive · the rounds sheet

Twenty-eight rows, one per station item

Check compares each entry with the plant now: numbers within a tolerance, states by exact choice.

Wherestation and level

A hand valve is moved only on the console's word: it changes the process.

Section summary

What part 3 settled

  • A tag reads as variable, function and loop number.
  • Identification without plates proves you know the plant.
  • The rounds sheet records numbers within a tolerance and states from a list.
  • Open vents, drains and bypasses raise no alarm: only a round finds them.

This deck

Key Takeaways

1

Walk the round water, steam, condensate, and know each station's level.

2

Use local gauges to confirm transmitters, and read a dial to a quarter division.

3

Keep blocks open and bypasses, vents and drains closed unless told otherwise.

4

Treat every hand-valve move as a process change the console must know.

5

Report tag, value, normal and action in one line.
